en: The Saṃyukta Āgama, with the Records of the Wu and Wei Dynasties, Part 1 (1).
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala, traveling together with a great number of bhikṣus.
He went into a bamboo grove and stayed within one of the bamboos; his movements were confined to the space between the cypress trees in the marsh.
At that time, there was a Brahmin farmer surnamed Pulu who, together with many plowmen outside the bamboo grove, gathered for a meal; he was capable of managing five hundred plows.
At that time, the Buddha thought, "It is still early; I shall now go to the dwelling of a farmer located at the front of this bamboo grove.
He arrived at the place where the farmers who possessed many plows were gathered for their mealtime assembly. The Buddha then went to the site of the farmers' meal assembly.
When the farmer saw that the Buddha had come, he spoke thus to him:
"I plow and sow for myself; having plowed and sown for myself, I eat.
You, who are a practitioner of discourse, may plow and sow; having plowed and sown, you shall eat."
The Buddha replied to the farmer in this way:
“I too plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat.
The farmer replied to the Buddha in this way:
"Although the Buddha has spoken thus, I plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat.
I do not see your implements for sowing—whether oxen, yokes, shafts, or plowshares—but merely speak of the farmer who sows, until the speech is cut off from behind."
"I do not see the implements for sowing; tell me the implements for sowing so that I may know how to sow.

The Buddha replied: "Faith is the seed; conduct is the water; wisdom is the ox; a sense of shame is the plow; the mind is the yoke-pin; the intellect is the golden [plowshare]; guarding the body and guarding speech is the furrow; sincerity and ceaseless cultivation bring it to completion; diligence does not abandon the pole; practicing these practices leads to peace; once these practices are performed, there is no returning; in these practices, there is no sorrow."
"Having thus sown, one shall thereby attain the Deathless;
by sowing thus, all shall be liberated from suffering.
Then the householder, with a vessel full of rice, approached the Buddha and offered it to him.
"The True Buddha can plow; the Real Buddha is a great plowman. I pray that you will accept my offering out of compassion.
The Buddha replied thus:
"Because the sutra has already been preached, it is not to be eaten; the practitioner has personally realized this Dharma through inquiry."

The Buddha has taught that the nature of phenomena is thus: one need not expect to attain the Way merely through the increase of phenomena; rather, it is through the exhaustion of fetters, the severing of doubt, and the establishment of mindfulness that this occurs.
Just as food, drink, offerings, and sacrifices are provided, so too does one enter this state and receive great merit therein.
The brāhmaṇa spoke again to the Buddha:
"To whom shall I now give this food?
The Buddha replied as follows:

"There is no one in the world—whether among gods, Māras, Brahmās, or śramaṇas—who could cause this food to remain undigested; however, the Buddha, who has also attained the Way, took this food and went to a place where there was water free of insects and cast it therein, or, if it were an open space without grass, he dug it up and buried it."

Having received the Buddha’s words, the brahmin departed and poured [the water] into it; as soon as he had poured it in, smoke issued forth, and it bubbled, seethed, and boiled violently with a sound. It was like a lump of glowing iron leaf heated for a day in a fire, which, when thrown into water, becomes hot, emits steam, bubbles, seethes, boils violently, and makes a sound.
When the brahmin had thus placed the rice into the water, smoke immediately issued forth, and it began to boil and bubble up with a great roar.
The brahmin was struck with terror and his hair stood on end; he then prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“May I become a śramaṇa under the Buddha, leave behind evil, receive the instructions and admonitions, and practice according to what I have received from the Buddha.”
The Buddha said,
"Once you have purified your practice of the Path, you shall follow from here.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction and admonition, the brahmin followed the Dharma until he attained the Path of Non-attachment.
The Buddha spoke thus.
(2) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa approached the Buddha.
Having arrived, he inquired after the Buddha’s well-being and sat down to one side.
Once seated to one side, Jātiśroṇa spoke thus to the Buddha:
"I have heard the Buddha say this:
'One should give to me alone; one must not give to others. Giving to me brings great merit, whereas giving to others does not bring great merit.'"
Give alms only to my disciples; do not give alms to the disciples of others. Giving alms to my disciples brings great merit; giving alms to the disciples of others does not bring such great merit.
"If one speaks in this way, is it for the sake of giving alms to me, or is it for the sake of giving alms to my disciples that there is great merit?
If one were to speak thus, would that not be reviling the Buddha and engaging in improper discourse? Is this the word of the Buddha?"
"Is it not as you have spoken? Have you not spoken according to the Dharma?
Have you not transgressed the Dharma?"
"Is there no way to obtain long or short [results]?
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"If a person says, 'The Buddha speaks thus: give alms only to me and do not give to others; give alms only to my disciples and do not give to others; giving alms to me brings great merit, while giving alms to other disciples brings little merit.'"

Thus, what is spoken does not accord with what is said; it is the exposition of my own treatise, which neither accords with what is said nor conforms to the Dharma—namely, the various treatises on phenomena. Why is this so?
I do not say such a thing as, "Give to me, but do not give to others," as stated above.
If one were to speak thus, it would destroy the path free from the three inversions; it would ruin the merit of the donor's household, ruin the virtue of the recipient, and also ruin one's own mind.
If there are scraps from the cauldron or the basin, one should take them to the garden and discard them there, with the thought:
"May the insects in the garden eat this; may their bodies be at peace and live thereby."
"For this reason, I say that one can thereby bring about merit.
Why then do you ask about giving to others?
I simply say:"
"One who maintains the precepts gains great merit; one who does not maintain the precepts gains little merit.
The brahmin replied to the Buddha, "I also say this:
one who maintains the precepts gains great merit; one who does not maintain the precepts gains little merit."

“One should give gifts to all according to their wishes. Those who do not observe the precepts have little merit; those who observe the precepts have great merit. Whether black, white, red, or yellow, it is the same for all that they practice—whether they be peacocks, oxen, or pigeons.”

This body arises according to its fundamental cause; its strength comes from the accumulation [of karma], and its good or evil issues from it. One should simply follow its course and not fixate on its outward appearance. Human beings are likewise:

all those who have taken birth in this body—whether they be practitioners of the Way, city-dwellers, farmers, or those of the lowest castes—each possesses a body born from these same conditions. Those who uphold the precepts can attain transcendence of the world; this constitutes great merit for them. As for the deluded who fail to understand, they do not hear what is difficult to accept; thus, they possess little merit.

There is nothing one does not know; however, it is the disciples of the Way who possess much wisdom regarding what they do know. These disciples of the Way have many branches rooted in faith: there are causes and conditions by which one ascends to the heavens through those causes and conditions; there are causes and conditions by which one falls into the evil realms through those causes and conditions; and there are causes and conditions by which one transcends the world through those causes and conditions—all such things proceed from causes and conditions.
The Brahmin Jātiśroṇa rose from his seat, placed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said: "From this day forth, I take refuge in the Buddha and observe the precepts.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
3. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There was a young Brahmin named Māṭhara who went to where the Buddha was. Having approached and exchanged greetings with the Buddha, he sat down to one side. Once seated, he questioned the Buddha:
“Holding such [a view], how does one analytically contemplate a wicked person?
The Buddha replied,
“For example, a wicked person is like the moon.”
He asked the Buddha again:
"If one wishes to distinguish a person of wisdom, what kind of contemplation should they maintain?
"The analogy for a person of wisdom is like the moon."
He asked the Buddha again:
"In what way is an unwise person like the moon?

"The Buddha replied: 'It is like the moon on the twenty-ninth day; its brightness diminishes, its color diminishes, its shape diminishes, and its visibility diminishes. As it passes through the middle of the night, it is in a state of waning. At times, the moon becomes entirely exhausted and no longer appears, as when the moon has reached its end.'"

Ignorance is likewise: for one who has heard the scriptural instructions and attained wisdom and faith through the path they have followed, yet does not practice them, does not receive them with heedfulness, and does not fix them in the mind—abandoning the teaching and failing to apply it—their faith diminishes, their virtue diminishes, their learning diminishes, their generosity diminishes, and their wisdom diminishes as the middle watch of the night passes away.

At one time, this brahmin caused those whom he had deluded to exhaust all [defilements] and no longer manifest anything, thereby attaining the excellent Dharma; it was like the twenty-ninth day when the moon has waned. Thus, the sight of these deluded ones is likened to the moon.
He asked the Buddha again:
"I wish to know the practice and teaching of one who possesses wisdom. The Buddha replied:

"It is like the moon on the fifteenth day; its brightness increases, its shape increases, and its visibility increases, until at that single moment the moon is fully perfected in all its growth. On the fifteenth day, it is also thus."

When a wise person’s words are moral and their conduct accords with the Dharma, they gain faith. From that faith, they listen to the teachings with focused attention and do not abandon them; they gather what has been taught and thereby increase their faith, increase their virtue, increase their learning, increase their generosity, and increase their wisdom. When these qualities have increased, they reach fulfillment even in the middle of the night, and at certain times they attain further growth. This is the complete perfection of all practices for a wise person, whose conduct is pure and whose instructions are refined. It is like the bright moon on the fifteenth day when the full moon has arrived; a person of clear wisdom perceives it in this way.

Brahmin, it is like the moon moving through its phases until its light ceases; just as when the bright moon travels in the midst of the sky, all the stars of the world are outshone by its brilliance, so too is it with one who has faith and learning: being able to practice giving without stinginess, they surpass all that is difficult to renounce in the world through the radiance of their generosity. It is like thunder, clouds, and lightning together, holding much water and sprinkling it upon the earth; so too is it with one who has faith and learning: being able to practice giving without stinginess, they provide food and drink in abundance and continue to bestow more. Thus, their fame and reputation fall like rain from the heavens, and those who receive this great merit obtain it just as rain brings down treasures and grain. Through such fame, one attains the celestial realms; having already cultivated virtuous conduct, one dwells in the heavens in future lives.
Thereupon, Bakkula rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet in salutation, and from this day forth accepted the Buddha’s instructions and practice.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
4. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"At one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Uruvelā, by the river named Nerañjarā, under a banyan tree on its bank. Having just attained the Way, he thought to himself:
'If a person practices the path alone, leading themselves as a practitioner, they can transcend sorrow, affliction, suffering, and the disagreeable, and attain liberation and the True Dharma.'"
What is the True Dharma?
It is the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?

If a bhikṣu practices the application of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body, he personally realizes that it is disagreeable due to worldly delusion and is able to remain detached from the contemplation of the signs of the body in the external body; he likewise practices the application of mindfulness by contemplating the signs of the body in the internal body and the external body, personally realizing that they are disagreeable due to worldly delusion. He is also able to remain detached from feelings, the mind, and dharmas in the same manner.

If a practitioner departs from the four foundations of mindfulness, they depart from the practice of the Dharma; having departed from the practice of the Dharma, they depart from the path of practice; having departed from the path of practice, they depart from the Deathless (amṛta). Having departed from the Deathless, they cannot transcend birth, old age, death, and affliction; nor can they transcend suffering, nor attain the essential goal.

If a practitioner possesses the four foundations of mindfulness and is able to cross over, they will then be able to undertake the practice of one who has attained the Way; having been able to undertake the practice of one who has attained the Way, they will then be able to attain the Way; having attained the Way, they will then be able to extinguish old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and affliction, and will then be able to achieve deliverance from suffering and also obtain the essential purity of Brahma, thereby knowing what I have contemplated.

Just as a strong man might extend his arm, bend it, and then extend it again, so too did Brahmā descend from the heavens and stand before me. Having stood there, he spoke to me in accordance with what the Buddha has reflected upon and what the Buddha has spoken: "The Path is the singular means for attaining purity, for becoming free from sorrow, distress, suffering, and the unpleasant;

it enables one to reach cessation and attain the True Dharma. It leads to the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). By practicing the foundation of mindfulness regarding the body as body, one knows through one's own mind how to become free from the delusions and the unpleasant of the world. One practices the foundation of mindfulness by observing the body externally, and by observing the body both internally and externally. Through this practice, one knows through one's own mind how to become free from the delusions and the unpleasant of the world. This applies likewise to feelings, the mind, and phenomena."

If a practitioner departs from the four intentions, they depart from the practice of the Dharma; having departed from the practice of the Dharma, they depart from the path of cultivation; having departed from the path of cultivation, they depart from the Deathless (Amṛta); having departed from the Deathless, they cannot depart from birth, old age, death, grief, and affliction, nor can they depart from suffering, nor can they attain the end of suffering. This is what is meant by knowing the skillful means of this practice.

"The goose’s foot was once drawn up in the water; let the Buddha himself proclaim my right practice. Simply accepting these words, one should make them one's own reckoning, as the sole means to lift oneself from the anxieties of birth and death."

Because one departs from the path of the heterodox teachings out of compassion, and because one has already attained transcendence of the world through this, and because both present and future deliverances likewise proceed from this—this is the fundamental purity of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is also through this that birth, old age, and death are exhausted. By practicing in reliance upon these various dharmas, this is what the possessor of the Eye of the Path has taught.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(5) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, while it was naturally bright and the night was also luminous, Brahmā approached the Buddha. At that moment, the Buddha was traveling by means of the supernormal power of fire. Then Brahmā thought:
"It is still early to go see the Buddha; now the Buddha is traveling by the supernormal power of fire, so let me now go before him."
He went to the Kukkutika monks of the Devadatta faction, and having approached them from afar, he addressed the Kukkutika monks of the Devadatta faction, saying:
"O Kukkutikas! Thus it is!"
Kubjita said to the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, as well as to other wise practitioners of the path, "You hold good intentions.
Kubjita, a follower of the Devadatta faction, then asked, "Who are you?"
The Brahmā said, "I am Brahmā.
The members of the Pūraṇa-Kāśyapa school replied:
"Did the Buddha say that you are an Anāgāmin?
Brahmā replied, "Yes."
The Kūṭadantīya school replied,
"By what causes and conditions have you come to this place?
Then he entered into Brahma-like contemplation and reflection.
"Why is it that they have no sense of compassion?
He then spoke this verse in Brahma-language:
"To measure the immeasurable— For this reason, the world lacks wisdom. To attempt to measure the immeasurable— In this way, the world covers itself."
He then practiced the Brahma-faring and went to the Buddha; having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side.
Having sat to one side, he spoke to the Buddha from his state as a Brahmā:
"I was my own light, and the night had already become bright when I came to the Buddha. When I arrived, the fire-god was walking on foot, and I thought to myself:"
"It is still too early to see the Buddha.

Having arrived at the Fire Deity’s supernormal power, I thought to myself, "May I go before them. I then went to the group of Kevaddha monks at Kevaddha Village. Having arrived at the group of Kevaddha monks at Kevaddha Village, I addressed them:
"Kevaddhas, Kevaddhas! You should maintain a friendly mind toward the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, who are fellow travelers on the Path."
He then asked: "Who are you? I replied:
"Brahmā," he replied to me,
"Does the Buddha say that you are an Anāgāmin?"
I replied, "It is so," and then he said:
"By what causes and conditions have you come to this place?
Then I reflected and thought: "Alas!"
"Why is it that they have no sense of compassion?

"They attempt to measure what is immeasurable; therefore, those in the world possess little wisdom. They attempt to define what cannot be defined; people of the world reckon with their own minds, thinking 'I know'."
The Buddha then spoke:
“Kūṭadanta, the faction of Devadatta is broken and defeated.
At that time, he uttered this verse:

"Those who attempt to measure the immeasurable, for this reason, find wisdom difficult to attain in the world; those who describe the immeasurable as measurable thereby shroud themselves in darkness."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(6) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are three skillful means for managing a livelihood: that which has not yet brought profit can be brought about, and that which has already been brought about does not diminish.
What are these three?..."

Among these monks, there are those who engage in worldly livelihoods; at dawn they contemplate many skillful means and exert their full strength toward their livelihood, and it is the same at midday and the same at evening, seeking many skillful means and exerting all their strength to ensure they obtain profit.
The three dharmas for a bhikṣu’s livelihood are also like this: he is able to attain the Dharma not yet attained, and he does not diminish the Dharma already attained.
What are these three?

Among these bhikṣus, there are bhikṣus who, in the morning, extensively cultivate the path with a mind of contemplation that does not depart from it; at midday and in the afternoon they do likewise, extensively uniting their minds in meditative concentration and practicing with a mind that does not depart from it, thereby being able to greatly increase the path.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(7) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Asatkāra who resided in the kingdom of Rājagṛha. Then Asatkāra thought to himself:

"The śramaṇa Kūṭadanta dwells in the Bamboo Grove at the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground in the kingdom of Rājagṛha. I shall now go to the śramaṇa Kūṭadanta; whatever sūtra the śramaṇa Kūṭadanta preaches, I shall refute it all and show my lack of faith."

Lacking faith and respect, he departed from Rājagṛha for the place where the Buddha was. At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by an assembly of more than a hundred people, seated in a circle, as he preached the Dharma-sūtra to them all.
The Buddha saw that Ajātaśatru was approaching from afar without faith or respect; having seen him, he stopped and did not preach the sutra.
When Ajātaśatru had arrived and paid his respects to the Buddha, they sat down together in one place. Once seated, Ajātaśatru said to the Buddha:
"I urge you, World-Honored One, to preach the sutra; I wish to hear it."
The Buddha replied:
“Brahmin, they do not have faith or respect.
Those who disregard this Dharma, those who do not understand the speaker, those whose minds are distracted, and those who wish to engage in dispute—[these are the ones].”
"If one seeks to be free from strife through the mind, yet delights in strife, and is able to join together anger and strife—it is such a person who can understand the Dharma discourse.
Having spoken thus, he did not believe or honor [the teaching], but rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and after paying homage, he reflected:

"I have awakened to the fact that I was foolish, deluded, ignorant, unskilled, and harbored evil intent when I came before the Tathāgata, the Arhat; having awakened, I wished to reject his words and refused to believe them."
"From this day forward, repenting of my past transgressions, I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, maintaining my original vows.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(8) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"I have also spoken of the Dharma for disciples in a summary; I have also explained it in full, yet it is difficult for those who find it hard to understand.
Śāriputra then addressed the Buddha:
"It may be spoken in summary, and it may also be explained fully regarding the Dharma for disciples; there will be those among the assembly of disciples who can understand it."
The Buddha then addressed Śāriputra:

"You should train yourself in this way: regarding all thoughts associated with the body-consciousness that are external—'this is I,' 'this is mine'—the underlying tendency of conceit shall no longer exist. Through the liberation of mind and the liberation by wisdom, one personally sees the Dharma, personally understands it, and personally realizes its attainment. Thus, regarding all thoughts associated with the body-consciousness that are external—'this is I,' 'this is mine'—the underlying tendency of conceit shall no longer exist."

If, Śāriputra, a bhikṣu, while possessing this body-consciousness, also contemplates externally that "all this is I, this is mine," then the underlying tendencies of pride will no longer exist; he attains liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and through the practice of wisdom regarding the Dharma, he personally sees and knows for himself the cessation of seeking and practice.

"Śāriputra, this is what is meant by a bhikṣu who is unattached, whose outflows are exhausted, who has reached the end of training, and who has transcended the world; it is for this reason that I have spoken these words.
Thus he spoke, concluding the discourse.

“The World-transcender’s teaching does not lead to mere words; it destroys desire and the thoughts of desire. The mind cannot remain thus [in delusion]; it also removes the slumber of ignorance and eliminates the knots of doubt. By contemplating the mind, one attains purity; this is the fundamental contemplation of the Dharma. Having explained the wisdom that transcends the world, he has also explained the destruction of delusion.”
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(9) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"This body consists of skin, flesh, marrow, blood, and raw meat, filled with excrement and urine; when you look upon this body, what do you see as beautiful?"
It constantly has nine apertures with foul diseases; it is perpetually impure, always fit for shame, and until old age and death, it is ever joined with enemies and accompanied by illness.
Why do you not loathe this body?
It must inevitably fall and must inevitably perish; once abandoned and buried in the earth, it will no longer be of use and will be devoured by foxes and wolves.
Why do you look upon it without shame? Who taught you to crave and lust after it?

As the Buddha said: "One should observe this within one's own mind: it is like a butcher’s block or a butcher’s table for a heap of bones; it is like being burned by fire or afflicted by poison. Foolish people take pleasure in it and do not realize it themselves; why do they not fear this snare? To be greedy and lustful is indeed folly!"

Wealth, grain, gold, silver, oxen, horses, slaves, and servants are sought for the sake of life; yet life exists only in the space between breaths, and even one's own fundamental nature is meager. Even a maximum lifespan of over a hundred years is but a confluence of suffering.
When one contemplates who it is that is subject to death:

as time passes, life gradually diminishes; the days of life come to an end together with the passing of time. Like a swift-flowing river, like the waning of the sun and moon, life rapidly passes away.
Human life once gone does not return; thus it is something that cannot be regained. When a person dies, their life-force departs.

Even if one possesses various riches, treasures, or celestial rarities, at the time of death all these confront one; they bring neither joy nor relief, neither weariness nor pleasure, and one finds no self-satisfaction therein. There is nothing else but what one has done well for oneself; there is nothing else but the good deeds one has performed by oneself, which naturally follow from oneself.
If one perceives death through knowledge and vision, what kind of person could possibly succumb to lust?
Whether one lives for a long time or passes away, one must eventually die; why, then, do you seek sensual pleasures with your mind?

Why is this? Because one does not dwell upon the thought of stillness; though one’s beloved child has died and one weeps for no more than ten days, once those ten days have passed, one forgets them. It is the same for a beloved wife, and it is likewise for one's household, kinsmen, and acquaintances.

Wealth is acquired through the suffering of birth; at the time of death, people inevitably abandon it. Though one cherishes one's own body and life, when they are entangled in the snares of existence, they are cast away; one enters beneath the earth, departing as a mere aggregate of the elements. Birth and decay follow the person like the fruit of a tree.
Having seen this, how could one who possesses conditioned things find contentment within them?

Among all the myriad things in the world, no single person can be satisfied; even if one were to obtain a portion of them, how could one ever feel weary of seeking more? Since there is no end to the five worldly pleasures through which one seeks self-indulgence across countless lifetimes, what kind of benefit would such a person bring to others?

Having already encountered those who suffer for their transgressions and experience the retribution of their deeds, one should act for the sake of benefiting them; one does not wish to undergo the tranquility of seeking [liberation] as a snake for oneself—just as it is with "little" and "much," so it is with "few" and "many."

Just as a disease is painful regardless of whether it is great or small, and just as a dog that finds a bone devoid of flesh will gnaw upon it without satiety—so too is this habituation to desire difficult to abandon; once obtained, one should regard it with great fear.

Those who do not abandon their habitual practices will likewise fall into evil states. It is like a person who, having seen a dream, awakens and no longer feels desire for it; likewise, one should view intense dreams as being devoid of true pleasure. Like a black viper, like meat for the starving, or like the fruit of a tree that yields little substance but much decay, such people increase their fetters and serve as the root of evil deeds. The practitioners of the Way do not employ such persons. Even when dwelling in the blissful abodes of the heavens, amidst the celestial trees of exquisite form, within palaces as beautiful as gardens, and even having obtained celestial princesses—having already failed to find satiety with these five heavenly pleasures, how could one now ever find weariness with the world?

It consists of two hundred bones—specifically one hundred and twenty segments—bound together by sinews; it is a vessel from which nine apertures constantly leak; it is the culmination of ninety-three types of ailments and a hundred diseases; it is a mixture of flesh and blood, and the site where skin and muscle grow; it is the locus for internal cold, heat, and wind; it is filled with excrement and urine, and hosts a thousand parasites—all of which arise from the body. Furthermore, within it there are a thousand orifices that are intensely painful: it causes harm to others once one has become attached to it; it produces impurities, with mucus flowing from the nose, saliva and spittle from the mouth, sweat from the armpits, and excrement and urine from the various apertures. Thus, all manner of suffering issues forth from this body.

A corpse in a cemetery is truly loathsome; it is likewise loathsome behind one's house, for it is the source of all impurities. From its very origin, it is like gold-plated [vessels], yet for the sake of clothing, it is smeared with perfumes, powders, unguents, dregs, red cotton, indigo, and collyrium. When foolish people see this, their minds become distracted—like a painted jar or a pit covered with grass—which they embrace with affection, only to feel regret later when it is gone.
The bhikṣu knelt and bowed, receiving the instruction as follows.
10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Bhikṣus, listen!
“We receive your instruction,” they replied.
The Buddha then said:
"Monks, there are four causes and conditions by which a person’s craving becomes either light or heavy, thereby departing from the Path.

Monks, it is like a man who has four wives. The first wife is highly esteemed by her husband; whether sitting, rising, walking, moving, lying down, or resting, she is never separated from him. When he bathes, adorns himself, or partakes of food, he always provides her with the five pleasures first. Whether in cold or heat, hunger or thirst, he massages, complies with, and protects her, never contending with her against her wishes."

As for the second wife, she sits, rises, and converses constantly by one's side; those who obtain her are joyful, while those who do not are sorrowful; she may lead to old age and illness, or even to strife and litigation.

As for the third wife, they would meet together from time to time; they frequently inquired after one another’s well-being and indulged their desires regarding what was bitter or sweet. Yet, when they became utterly exhausted and emaciated by poverty, they grew weary of and disgusted with one another, sometimes distancing themselves until they longed for each other again upon meeting.

The fourth wife was in charge of providing service and errands; whenever there were tasks requiring haste or various difficult and painful labors, she would immediately go to attend to them. Yet he neither questioned her nor spoke with her, rarely looking after her and keeping her out of his mind.
Once these four wives' husbands encountered a matter of death and were about to be exiled far away, they called to the first wife, saying:
"You must follow me.
The first wife replied:
"I will not follow you," [the wife] said. Her husband replied, "My deep love for you is peerless;
whether in great or small matters, much or little, I have always followed your wishes. I have nurtured and protected you so as never to fail your intent—for what reason would I not follow you?"
The wife said,
"Though you hold me in great affection and esteem, I ultimately cannot go with you.
The husband then departed in resentment and called for his second wife:
"You should follow me," he said.
The second wife replied, "Even your most cherished and beloved first wife will not follow you; I certainly will not follow you either."
The husband said:

"When I first sought you, my toil and suffering were beyond description; I endured cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and further faced water, fire, government officials, and bandits, contending with others through cleverness and sharp wit before I finally obtained you. Why then do you not follow me?"
The wife said, "You yourself were greedy for profit and forced me to seek you; I did not seek you out. Why do you speak to me with such weary persistence?
The husband then left in resentment and called for his third wife:
"You should follow me.
The third wife replied: "I have received your kindness;
I shall escort you to the outskirts of the city, but I cannot travel further to reach the place where you intend to go."
Feeling such resentment within himself, he returned and consulted with his fourth wife, saying:
"I shall depart from this kingdom; you must follow me.
The fourth wife replied:
"I have originally left my parents to come here to serve you as your attendant; whether in life or death, in sorrow or joy, I shall follow wherever you go.
Yet this husband was unable to take his three beloved and esteemed wives with him; he could only depart together with one who was bitter, ugly, and disagreeable.

The Buddha said: "Regarding the parable I have just related: the 'one person' is the conscious spirit (manas) of a human being; the 'first wife' represents the human body. A person loves their own body more than that first wife. Yet when life ends in death, the conscious spirit must depart alone for far away, following its karma of merit and demerit; the body lies stiff upon the ground, unwilling to follow."
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu cannot attain liberation without following four practices.
What are these four?"
First is sorrow and suffering; second is the pursuit of desire; third is the emptiness of exhaustion; and fourth is the eradication of all evils.
The essentials of the Way consist of eight practices, and sincere devotion lies in the Four Noble Truths.

The second wife is a person's property; those who obtain her rejoice, while those who do not grieve. Yet when life comes to its end, wealth and treasures remain behind in the world, and one cannot take them with oneself, sitting in vain sorrow and suffering.

The third kind of wife refers to parents, wives, children, brothers, the five types of close relatives, acquaintances, and servants; because of the affection and love generated during life, they long for one another with mutual longing until, at the end of life, they weep as they escort the deceased to the cemetery outside the city, where they immediately abandon the dead and return to their own homes. Their grief does not last beyond ten days, after which they resume eating and drinking together, having cast the memory of the dead aside.

The fourth wife is the human mind. There is no one in the world who loves and protects their own mind; instead, all let their minds run wild and indulge them in greed, anger, and a lack of faith in the Right Path. When the body dies, they shall fall into the evil realms—whether entering hell, becoming an animal, or becoming a hungry ghost—all of which result from the indulgence of the mind.

"Monks! For the sake of the Path, you should rectify your own minds and align your intentions; you should eliminate the mind of delusion and act without delusion. Cease and do not commit evil; by not committing evil, one does not receive calamity. Not receiving calamity, one is not born; not being born, one does not age; not aging, one does not fall ill; not falling ill, one does not die. By not dying, one attains the unconditioned path of Nirvana."
The Buddha spoke thus as the Tathatā; the bhikṣus received it with joy.
11 (11) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Rājagṛha. The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:

"When people dwell in this world, if one were to collect the bones from their births and deaths throughout a single kalpa—bones that do not decay, dissolve, or perish—and pile them up until they equal Mount Sumeru; or if some person undergoes births and deaths for a hundred kalpas, or even a thousand kalpas—they may still not yet attain the path of Arhatship and Nirvana."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If one were to collect the bones of a person over the course of a kalpa, they would equal Mount Sumeru; for this reason, I have manifested their original causes and conditions."

"Monks! You all must uproot the very foundation and depart from that foundation. For this reason, you will no longer undergo birth and death; by no longer undergoing birth and death, you shall attain the path of Nirvana, which transcends the world."
Thus spoke the Buddha. (12) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus responded.
"So be it. We shall receive the Buddha's words.
The Buddha then spoke:

“Regarding form, bhikkhus, one reflects upon its origination as suffering, reflects upon its impermanence and its dissolution; having gone forth and observed it thus, a bhikkhu is able to observe form correctly. If one can know the reflection upon the origination of form, if one can know the impermanence and dissolution of form, and if one can know correct observation, then craving for form will depart.”
Once the craving for form has been destroyed, craving and greed are likewise destroyed; once craving and greed are destroyed, the mind is liberated. This is what I have taught.

Regarding feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, a bhikkhu should reflect upon their origin and also reflect upon consciousness as impermanent. He should also contemplate them with discernment. If a bhikkhu has reached such discernment and has abandoned craving, then with the exhaustion of craving, craving and greed are exhausted, and he is thus liberated from birth and death and attains the Path.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (13) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall explain to you from what evil arises, and likewise explain from what goodness arises.
Bhikṣus, listen and apply your minds with careful attention."
The bhikṣu should reply:
"Indeed. [The Buddha asked:
"What is the nature of this evil intent?"
When greed for past, future, or present forms gives rise to self-loathing, fear, and delusion, and when all views and evil intentions arise toward them, these are called "the loathsome.
It is the same for sensations, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness.
This is called that which arises from evil.
What is meant by "wholesome intention"?

Regarding form—past, future, or present—if one does not give rise to views, and is without ill will, without fear, and without delusion, and is free from all afflictive and malicious intentions, this is called wholesome intention. It is likewise with feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
The Buddha said:
"What I have taught regarding good and evil intentions is thus.
14 (14) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four foundations of mindfulness.”
What are the four?

There is a bhikṣu who dwells contemplating the body within the body, exerting his full effort, clearly knowing it with mindfulness, and remaining undeluded; for delusion is the root of sorrow in the world.
Regarding the external body, one dwells in contemplation of the body with diligent effort; now knowing this, the mind does not forget, emerging from delusion, for delusion brings sorrow to the world.

Regarding both the internal and external body, one dwells in contemplation of the body with diligent effort; now knowing this, the mind does not forget, emerging from delusion, for delusion brings sorrow to the world.

Internally, when experiencing painful or itchy sensations, one observes these painful or itchy sensations with equanimity; exerting oneself, one now knows this state of mind and does not forget it as it emerges from delusion, yet it becomes a source of sorrow for the world.

Externally, when experiencing painful or itchy sensations, one observes these painful or itchy sensations with equanimity; exerting oneself, one now knows this state of mind and does not forget it as it emerges from delusion, yet it becomes a source of sorrow for the world.

One dwells contemplating the internal and external sensations as sensations; exerting one's full effort, one now knows them, remains mindful, and does not forget, emerging from delusion, yet remains concerned for the world.
One dwells contemplating the internal mind as mind; exerting one's full effort, one now knows it, remains mindful, and does not forget, emerging from delusion, yet remains concerned for the world.

One contemplates the mind with the external mind, bringing it to stillness; exerting all effort, one now knows the mind and does not forget it, emerging from delusion, yet remains a source of sorrow for the world.

One contemplates the mind with both the internal and external mind, bringing it to stillness; exerting all effort, one now knows the mind and does not forget it, emerging from delusion, yet remains a source of sorrow for the world.

Internally, through the practice of *saṃvega* regarding the phenomena of the True Dharma, one exerts all effort to now know the mind, not forgetting it, and emerging from delusion; this is for the sake of the world’s sorrow.

Internally and externally, through the practice of *saṃvega* regarding the phenomena of the True Dharma, one exerts all effort to now know the mind, not forgetting it, and emerging from delusion; this is for the sake of the world’s sorrow.

Regarding the internal and external dharmas, one contemplates the characteristics of each dharma with both calming (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā). Exerting all effort, one now knows that the mind does not forget its emergence from delusion, which is the cause of the world’s suffering.

The Buddha has thus taught these four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni); the disciples of the Buddha should receive and practice them, applying themselves with diligence to attain the Way.
15 (15) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:

“There is this one dharma for a bhikkhu, which, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed as a mental orientation, leads to tranquility of body, is attended to by the mind, and brings about cessation without remainder; it is simply mindfulness directed toward the principles of skillful conduct, accompanied by the recollection of the Dharma.”
What is this one dharma?
It is the practice of *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).

If a bhikṣu practices *ānāpānasmṛti*, maintains mindfulness, and dwells frequently therein, his body attains tranquility, and his mind likewise becomes mindful and composed; thus, [distractions] cease and no longer exist. He then possesses wise mindfulness, and his practice of the Dharma becomes fulfilled and perfected. This is the one dharma of a bhikṣu.

By means of a single characteristic of phenomena, one immediately practices the characteristic of conduct; for the sake of attaining rest for the body, one takes the characteristics of the mind as objects of mindfulness and waits for them. Thus, there is cessation without remainder; one merely practices with wisdom, and the practice of mindfulness of phenomena increases and becomes full.
"If a bhikṣu is able to practice, master, recollect, and cultivate this one dharma, he shall attain the Path.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (16) It was heard thus:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two powers by which one attains the supreme path.
What are these two powers?"
This refers to the power of restraint through understanding and the power of guarding the mind.
What is meant by the power of restraint through understanding?

This is what the true disciple who has heard the Way understands: that practicing evil with the body leads to the acquisition of evil fortune; that if one commits evil with the body in this life or future lives, one will personally incur the offense and likewise afflict others; that what is not the path yet is followed by people, and constitutes a violation of the precepts; that people of the ten directions will speak ill of me, and I too will follow inauspicious speech; and that my body will perish and I shall fall into hell. This is what is called evil conduct of the body, which results in evil fortune. Such is the evil in this life, and such is the evil in future lives. Thus, one abandons evil bodily conduct for the sake of the body, maintains wholesome mindfulness to purify the body and reach the state of non-transgression. Likewise regarding transgressions of mind, this is called understanding the power of restraint.
What is the power of the practice of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*)?

It is that which is attained through guarding, that which is returned to through self-guarding, and the power of the practice of mindfulness regarding that which is stilled. This refers to the practice reaching its own destination and seeking attainment through mindfulness; this is called the power of the practice of mindfulness.
He spoke thus.
The bhikṣus rejoiced and rose to pay their respects.
17 (17) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three powers.”
What are the three powers?
First, the power of faith; second, the power of diligence; third, the power of wisdom.
What is the power of faith?

When a disciple of the Way possesses an intention for the Buddha-way that cannot be destroyed, they abide in the practice of the Buddha’s grace; they speak the words of the Buddha thus, according to truth and without attachment. Through truthful awakening and wisdom, they attain joy—the Father of the World. Thus, having reached the Buddha and abandoned evil, they arrive at wise conduct; this is what is called the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).

What is the power of diligence (*vīryabala*)? It is when a bhikṣu, having already produced unwholesome thoughts, exerts himself to abandon them; he seeks to practice, strives, and maintains right mindfulness. He does not allow unarisen unwholesome thoughts to arise, and he seeks to produce unarisen wholesome thoughts. He stabilizes, does not forget, and does not diminish the dharmas that have already arisen, but causes them to increase day by day and multiply. Practicing with mindfulness, fulfilling his aspiration, seeking attainment, and exerting himself with a restrained mind until he emerges—this is called the power of diligence.
What is the power of wisdom?

If a bhikṣu, regarding this suffering and its origin as they truly are, knows the origin as the origin, knows suffering as suffering, knows the origin as the origin, and understands the cessation of suffering as the essential realization of the cessation of suffering—this is called the power of wisdom.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, and having heard it, the bhikṣus accepted and practiced it according to his instructions.
18 (18) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four powers.
What are these four powers?"
First is the power of intention, second is the power of diligence, third is the power of non-transgression, and fourth is the power of guarding.

What is the power of intention? If a bhikṣu knows good and evil turbidity as one would know it with utmost sincerity; if he knows what is transgression and what is not transgression; if he knows what is permissible and what is impermissible; if he knows what is deficient and what is increased; if he knows what is white and what is black; and if he knows how to attain purity and knows it as it truly is—this is called the power of intention.
What is the power of diligence?

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, amidst these corruptions, speaks what is evil, speaks what is transgressive, speaks what is improper, speaks what is dark, and speaks what is not for those who strive; such persons he abandons. If, however, amidst these corruptions, one speaks what is good, speaks what is non-transgressive, speaks what is to be practiced, speaks what is appropriate, speaks what is bright, and speaks what is the Path—then regarding such persons amidst these corruptions, does one act out of desire, or does one act with diligence, or does one apply the mind, or does one restrain the mind?
This is called the power of diligence.
What is the power of non-transgression?

There is a bhikṣu who practices restraint so as not to transgress with the body; he practices restraint so as not to transgress with speech; he practices restraint so as not to transgress with the mind. This is called the power of non-transgression.
What is the power of guarding?
It refers to the four groups.
What are the four groups?
"First is gathering [the community], second is giving, third is showing compassion, and fourth is assisting in virtuous conduct; these are called the powers of guarding.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
19 (Nineteen). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“People possess five powers that cause women to deceive men.
What are these five powers? First is beauty;
second is physical comeliness; third is having many male siblings; fourth is noble lineage; and fifth is great wealth.”
What is meant by "form" (rūpa)?
It refers to a woman who is unvirtuous; being unvirtuous, she does not wish to engage in productive livelihood.

She becomes prone to anger and is unwilling to maintain the household. Such a woman considers herself peerlessly beautiful, considers herself to have many brothers who are powerful, considers herself from a noble and wealthy family, and considers herself to possess abundant property—it is such a woman who is unvirtuous.

If there is a woman who is chaste and virtuous, free from the lusts of women, she maintains the two excellent teachings through great integrity. Having received these two excellent teachings, she desires to manage her household affairs, harbors no anger, and seeks to uphold the family. For one such as this, physical beauty is not required; thus, for such a person, it is simply the mind that serves others. She does not rely on the strength of many male brothers, nor on the pride of noble lineage or wealth, nor on vast possessions—her mind remains equanimous. Thus she receives the teaching, and having been taught, she maintains it well without slackening, desiring to manage her livelihood.

With a peaceful mind and no desire for anger, she does not abandon her household duties; rather, she desires to manage her livelihood and care for the family—such is the disposition of a virtuous woman.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (20) It was heard thus:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus!

Those who have not heard [the Dharma] associate, congregate, correspond, and find mutual approval with those who have not heard; those who have heard much associate, congregate, correspond, and find mutual approval with those who have heard much."

The stingy associate with, gather with, correspond to, and find approval in those who are like them in their stinginess; the generous associate with, gather with, correspond to, and find approval in those who are like them in their generosity;

the clever associate with, gather with, correspond to, and find approval in those who are like them in their cleverness; the deluded associate with, gather with, correspond to, and find approval in those who are like them in their delusion;

those with many desires associate with, gather with, correspond to, and find approval in those who are like them in their many desires; and those with few desires associate with, gather with, correspond to, and find approval in those who are like them in their few desires.

Those who are difficult to support are associated with, gathered together with, correspond to, and find mutual compatibility with those who are difficult to support; those who are easy to support are associated with, gathered together with, correspond to, and find mutual compatibility with those who are easy to support;

those who are difficult to provide for are associated with, gathered together with, correspond to, and find mutual compatibility with those who are difficult to provide for; those who are easy to provide for are associated with, gathered together with, correspond to, and find mutual compatibility with those who are easy to provide for;

those who are insufficient are associated with, gathered together with, correspond to, and find mutual compatibility with those who are insufficient; and those who are sufficient are associated with, gathered together with, correspond to, and find mutual compatibility with those who are sufficient.

Those who do not maintain [the precepts] are those who, being alike in nature, gather together, associate with one another, and find mutual approval; those who maintain [the precepts] are those who, being alike in nature, gather together, associate with one another, and find mutual approval.
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! Thus it is;
a wise person should discern these causal conditions: that which is to be practiced should be practiced, and that which is not to be practiced should not be practiced."
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the heavens, Śakra was formerly a human being; because he possessed seven vows—vows such as 'being as one has reached the end of life' and 'seeking to fulfill them as they were originally intended'—he is therefore called Śakra."
What are the seven?
One must, throughout one's life, be filial toward one's parents.
One must, throughout one's life, pay reverence to those who are aged.
One should not utter words that are like flames;
one should speak words in accordance with the Dharma;
and until the end of one's life, one should not harbor anger, nor engage in slander or false speech.

One should, for the sake of the ultimate goal, speak words of utmost sincerity; one should be joyful in utmost sincerity and restrained in utmost sincerity, always being trustworthy and not deceiving the world.
One should, for the sake of the ultimate goal, overcome the world’s stinginess; I shall ensure that within my own mind I do not follow the stinginess found in households.
To practice giving by opening one's hand and constantly granting what is requested is called "excellent giving" and is categorized as equal-part giving.

For the sake of becoming a Śakra Devendra, one dwells among humans in this world and makes these seven vows; it is taught that one must fully practice them until the end of life, for it is from this root that one attains the status of a Śakra.
He spoke further in verse:

"To be filial toward one's parents is the ancient rite of the noble clans; abandon burning passion, speak as you please, cast out slander and falsehoods, and emerge from stinginess to practice truth, patience, joy, and right speech."
"For this reason, one is able to attain rebirth in heaven; wherever people wish to practice this, they should perform the heavenly rite in this manner.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
22 (Twenty-two). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then took some soil with the tip of his fingernail and, having taken it, addressed the bhikṣus:
“Monks! How do you understand this?
What is it that is most abundant?”
"Compared to the earth, how much is the soil on the tip of a fingernail? The bhikṣu should then reply:

"The soil upon the Buddha’s fingernails is so little that it cannot be compared to the soil of the earth; there is no comparison. It is not even a hundredfold, nor a thousandfold, nor ten-thousandfold, nor a hundred-millionfold; it is beyond calculation, beyond all numerical analogy, and beyond aggregation. No metaphor can describe it—the soil of the earth is exceedingly vast."
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:

"The wisdom and insight-eye of such people as those who do not know is like the soil of the earth; the wisdom and insight-eye of such people as those who act upon it is like the soil on a fingernail."

Such is the conduct of one who acts with the eye of wisdom; thus may one train in the conduct of the eye of wisdom, for therein is no fault. Wisdom, once born, should serve as one's own sustenance; in this way, a bhikṣu who wishes to practice the Path may train.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
23 (23) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus: "The body is devoid of reciprocity; it does not acknowledge kindness.

If there is even a slight ailment that becomes an illness, the entire body suffers with it. It always seeks to obtain what it desires at will: giving the eyes fine forms, the ears pleasant sounds, the nose fragrant scents, the tongue delicious flavors, and the body soft textures. Though the body is nourished in this way, when it is abandoned and decays, it has no desire to save others."
"Why is this? Because they do not fully follow the rules of training, but merely commit transgressions.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“In a past age there was a king named Mahāpuṣpa, who, as he was about to die, said:
‘Alas! What use is this body? What should be done with it?’”
‘One may nurture and protect it with all one’s strength until the end of a hundred years, yet when the matter of death arrives, the body is immediately destroyed and decayed.
Thus, this body is devoid of any constancy; knowing this to be its nature, how could one possibly regard it as something to be cherished and nurtured?

There is suffering as severe as that of an enemy; one seeks out one's own transgressions, and upon encountering even slight pain, one immediately displays an attitude of anxiety. Though constantly provided with the five most excellent pleasures, when one observes them closely, they will inevitably lead to old age, sickness, and death.
"A bhikṣu should keep this in mind and not forget it; having understood this, he should practice it and teach it to others.
Thus the Buddha taught. 24 (24) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“The lion, king of beasts, emerges from his dwelling; having emerged from his dwelling, he yawns; having yawned, he looks about and gazes in the four directions.”

He then proceeded three times with the lion’s roar, traveling wherever his mind directed him. Upon seeing that there were mountains and rivers within which it was deep and swift, making it difficult to cross, he, like a lion, halted by the side of a river. Then, having crossed over the edge, he established a perception and formed this mental intention:
"From here I shall descend to the sphere of consciousness and emerge from it."

Having descended, if he could not emerge from the place known to the lion king, he would immediately return; if he crossed it again and still could not emerge, he would return once more. He constantly sought to emerge from the place he recognized, yet until his death, the lion king did not let him go, nor did he move on, nor did he abandon him.

The same applies to the non-apprehension of what is cognized. There are foolish people who do not carefully receive what they have heard and studied; they speak to crowds for others' sake until they are led away. These foolish people do not abandon their state of folly, nor do they desire what is essential; they do not carefully receive the core requirements of the scriptures. If this is so, then a wise person should awaken to this:

"I must apply myself with the power of studying the scriptures; I must apply myself with the power of inquiry; I must apply myself with the power of diligent contemplative practice; I must remain unremitting. It is difficult to escape the dying state of a lion-king; few people awaken to the desire to practice the Way."
"One should train in this way.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (25) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the lecture hall in the kingdom of Rājagṛha.

At that time, a brahmin named Aśvalāyana approached the Buddha. Having arrived, he addressed the Buddha with coarse and wicked speech, reviling and scolding him most harshly. The Buddha then preached a sutra with parables for the brahmin Aśvalāyana:
"If a person is without evil, yet speaks toward them with wicked words, and possesses no pure conduct—this foolish and wicked person will thereby bring calamity upon himself."
"It is like a person walking against the wind who is covered by the dust it brings.
Thereupon, the Brahmin Aśvajit placed his head at [the Buddha's] feet and said: "I acknowledge my transgression and accept your reproach.

Like one who is deluded, like one who is foolish, like one who lacks understanding, and like one who lacks clarity—I am called a fool. For the sake of those who cross over the world, though you were reviled with wicked words, you repeatedly admonished me. May the Buddha accept my repentance for the sake of this foolish man; from now on, I shall restrain myself and never commit such an offense again."
The Buddha replied:

“Since the brahmin has already repented his transgression—acting as one who was foolish, deluded, ignorant, and lacking understanding by reviling the Tathāgata with foul words—and since he has seen his error, repented, and declared that he will henceforth restrain himself and not dare to offend again, this is an increase in the path of practice and not a decrease. If, having recognized his fault, he repents of his own accord, manifests his sincerity without concealment, maintains his original resolve, and does not offend again.”
The brahmin then took refuge in the Buddha.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(26) [Sūtra 26] It was heard thus:
At one time, when the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there was a brahmin named Adhicca who went to the Buddha's dwelling, conversed with him, and sat down together with him.
Having sat down in one place, the practitioner named Abhaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"My name is Abhaya.
The Buddha replied:
"Is the mind also like the name?
The Brahmin then replied:
"It does not transgress."
Following this, he spoke in verse:
"If one does not invade others with the body, And likewise with speech and a well-intentioned mind, Such a person is called 'one who does not invade';
To be without anything to invade is truly marvelous."

Thereupon, the practitioner who had not transgressed rose from his seat, placed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said: "From this day forth, I shall uphold the instruction and no longer violate the five precepts.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
27. The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Seven Bases and Three Contemplations (27). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then called to the bhikṣu: "Know the seven stations and contemplate the three stations;

swiftly abide in the Dharma of the Path to be liberated from the fetters. Being without fetters, the mind is liberated through wisdom and attains the Dharma. Having seen the Dharma and personally realized the Path, birth is exhausted; having practiced the intention of the Path and done what was to be done, one shall no longer return."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"What are the seven points?
You should understand them well."

"Having heard that a bhikṣu knows form as it truly is, he also knows the arising of form, the cessation of form, the practice leading to the extinction of form, the gratification of form, the suffering of form, and the escape from form; and he does so with utmost sincerity.

Likewise, he knows feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness as they truly are; he knows the arising of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness, the gratification of consciousness, the suffering of consciousness, and the escape from consciousness; and he does so with utmost sincerity regarding the very nature of consciousness."
What is the suchness of form as it truly is?

Form has the four great elements as its basis; it exists within the four great elements, and it is also contained within the four great elements. One should know the suchness of the basis of form as it truly is.
What is the arising of form as it is known as it was originally?
Craving is the arising of form; such is the knowledge of the arising of form.
What is the cessation of form as it is realized through sincerity?
To know the exhaustion of craving as the exhaustion of form—such knowing of the exhaustion of form is ultimate knowledge (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
What is the ultimate knowledge of the exhaustion of the formations of form?
If these forms constitute the eightfold path—namely, right view through to right concentration as the eighth—then such knowing of the practice that exhausts form is the basis of ultimate knowledge.
What is the knowledge of the gratification of form as it truly is?
Whatever desire arises, whatever delight arises, and whatever craving arises regarding form—this is the knowledge of the gratification of form as it truly is.
What is the thorough knowledge of form as it truly is, namely, as being distressing?
That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the thorough knowledge of form as it truly is, namely, as being distressing.
What is the essential knowledge of form as it truly is?
It is the ability to understand the desire and lust for form, to abandon that desire, and to transcend that desire; such is the essential knowledge of form as it truly is.
What is meant by "knowing feelings"?
There are six bases for feelings: the eye-base feeling, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-base feelings. This is what is meant by knowing feelings.
What is the arising of feeling?
The arising of the latent tendencies is the arising of feeling; such arising is the arising of feeling.
What is the full knowledge of the cessation of feeling?
When all sensations have been uprooted, one fully knows the exhaustion of sensation; such is the full knowledge of the exhaustion of sensation.
What is the practice regarding the experience of sensation?

If one undergoes the eightfold path—namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these constitute the eight. In this way, the practice of experiencing sensation until it is exhausted constitutes the Path.
What is the consciousness of the gratification of feeling?
It is the seeking of feeling, the coming of what is sought, and the delight therein; such is the knowledge of the gratification of feeling-consciousness.
What is the consciousness of the distress of feeling?
To regard feelings as impermanent, subject to decay, suffering, and subject to change—this is the perception of feelings as affliction.
What is the essential nature of feelings?

Whatever sensations of pain or pleasure arise, the capacity for craving and grasping to transcend them—this is what constitutes the essential nature of sensation; one must recognize it and know it as it truly is.
What is the consciousness of mental formations?
Regarding the six perceptions of the body: the perception of the eye-facet, and the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-facets; such are the perceptions of the six consciousnesses.
What is the perception of the accumulation of perceptions?
Cultivation through practice constitutes the cultivation of volitional formations; thus is there the consciousness of the cultivation of volitional formations.
What is the consciousness of the exhaustion of volitional formations?
The exhaustion of volitional formations constitutes the consciousness of the exhaustion of volitional formations; thus is there the consciousness of the exhaustion of volitional formations.
What is the consciousness of the complete exhaustion of ideation through practice?

This consists of the eightfold consciousness: consciousness, truth, vision, arrival, truth, concentration, intention, and the eighth; thus is there the complete exhaustion of ideation through the practice of consciousness.
What is the consciousness of the gratification of thought?
It is that which, conditioned by thought, gives rise to pleasure and the attainment of joy; such is the consciousness of the gratification of thought.
What is the consciousness of the affliction of thought?
The perception that thoughts are impermanent, subject to exhaustion, suffering, and subject to change—this is what constitutes the perception of the affliction of thought.
What is the essential perception of thought?

To be able to resolve what is thought and intended, to sever desire and greed, and to be able to cross over by means of overcoming desire and greed—this is what constitutes the essential knowledge of thought.
What is the knowledge of birth and death?

There are six bases for the consciousness of birth and death: the eye-base as the consciousness of birth and death, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases as formations; such are the consciousnesses of birth and death.
What is the accumulation of birth and death?
The cultivation of planting is the consciousness of the habituation to birth and death.
What is the consciousness of the exhaustion of birth and death?
The exhaustion of planting is the consciousness of the exhaustion of birth and death.
What is the consciousness of the practice of craving for the exhaustion of birth and death?

It consists of eight practices; namely, the eightfold path of right view through to right concentration—this is the consciousness of the practice of receiving [the fruits] for the cessation of birth and death.
What is the consciousness of the flavor of birth and death?
It is the arising of pleasure and joy within the mind due to the causes and conditions of birth and death; such is the consciousness of the flavor of birth and death.
What is the consciousness of the affliction of birth and death?
All that is subject to birth and death, impermanence, exhaustion, suffering, and transformation—this is the consciousness of the affliction of birth and death.
What is the essential consciousness of birth and death?

That which is for the purpose of avoiding craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*), severing craving for existence, and transcending craving for existence—this is what constitutes the essential knowledge of birth and death.
What is the consciousness-body of the six bases of decay (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*)?
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the bases for consciousness; thus it is called "consciousness as consciousness.
What is the origination of consciousness?
The origination of the life-force and name is the origination of consciousness; such is the origination of consciousness.
What is the exhaustion of consciousness as the activity of feeling?
When the designation of life is exhausted, that is the exhaustion of consciousness.
What is the exhaustion of consciousness as the activity of feeling?
The eightfold path consists of right view through to right concentration as the eighth; thus, it is the knowledge of the exhaustion of craving that acts according to the truth of consciousness.
What is the knowledge of the gratification of consciousness?
When, due to the causes and conditions of what is cognized, joy and gladness arise in the mind, such is the tasting that arises; this is known as the cognition of taste.
What is the cognition of affliction?
When what is cognized is understood as exhaustion, as suffering, and as transformation, such is the cognition of affliction.
What is essential knowledge? That which is known such that desire and greed can be countered, desire and greed can be severed, and one can cross over them—this is essential knowledge.
In this way, a bhikṣu attains awakening through these seven points.
What are the seven?
Form, arising, cessation, the path, gratification, suffering, and escape—these are the seven matters for each of the five aggregates.
What are the three contemplations?

Consciousness also has seven matters; by attaining the five aggregates, it constitutes six matters. Contemplating the body as one form, contemplating the five aggregates as two, and contemplating the six sense-bases as three—therefore, they are called the "three contemplations."

"Monks! One who can comprehend the seven bases and also practice the three contemplations will, before long, follow the path. Having severed the fetters, they will be free from the intention of bondage; having attained liberation through wisdom and seen the essential, they will realize the goal once and for all. Having brought an end to birth and death and completed what was to be done, they shall no longer return to fall into the cycle of birth and death, having attained the Way."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Saṃyukta Āgama*.
